subject: Plan simplification + rollback play for Medistack
messages:
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>
To: Claire Porter <claire@medistack.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: Wed, 05 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Plan simplification + rollback play for Medistack

Hi Claire —

Thanks again for the demo last week. I pulled together a simplified plan that addresses the main blockers you raised (price predictability, safe downgrade path, and feature bundling for your clinical pipelines). High-level proposal: 

- Two primary offering tiers for your deployment: Core (shared hosting) and Core+ (dedicated capacity + priority routing).
- Feature bundles: Real-time inference (per-call), KV-prefix caching (saves tokens on repeated prompts), and Priority Support (SLAs) are grouped in Core+; Core includes basic generation + embeddings.
- Pricing constructs: 12-month and 36-month commitment options. Year-1 starter pricing includes a limited onboarding credit.

Rollback / downgrade play (what you asked about):
- Downgrade window: customer may request downgrade to Core within the first 90 days of activation.
- Execution SLA: Redwood will enact downgrade within 72 hours of a signed change order.
- Credit mechanics: Pro-rated credit applied to remaining committed term on a per-seat/token pool basis; unused onboarding credits are forfeited.

I attached a simple pricing grid and a draft SOW so you can see the numbers and the operational steps (Medistack_pricing_grid_v1.xlsx, Medistack_SOW_draft_v2.pdf).

Questions for you:
1) Do you need the downgrade to preserve seat allocations (so you can re-upgrade without re-provisioning)?
2) Does procurement want fixed monthly invoices or quarterly (helps figure the pro-rata math)?

If useful, I can set a 30-minute call with Karthik (account lead) and Marissa (finance) to walk through the credit formula and finalize the SOW.

Thanks —

— Soojin Lee
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
soojin_lee@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0192

Thanks, Soojin. This is helpful — especially the explicit timeline for a downgrade. A couple clarifying items before we loop in procurement formally: 

- Credit calculation: can you confirm the exact formula? Example scenario: we commit to Core+ for 12 months, after 45 days we downgrade to Core. How is our unused commitment credited?
- Seat preservation: if we downgrade, do we retain seat mappings+permissions for 6 months so our team can re-upgrade without losing user mappings?
- Billing cadence: procurement prefers monthly invoices for now but may move to quarterly if it reduces admin overhead.

Also, we need to add a clause about data retention during rollback — especially around cached KV content and any temporary logs. Can Redwood confirm retention windows and access controls during the downgrade process?

If you can provide a clear example with numbers that procurement can sign off on quickly, that would speed things up. Happy to do a short call, CCing procurement.

Best,
Claire
Head of Platform Engineering, Medistack
claire@medistack.com

From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>
To: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: Fri, 07 Aug 2026 08:22:00 -0700
Subject: Fwd: Plan simplification + rollback play for Medistack — need final guidance on credits/retention

Karthik / Marissa —

Forwarding Claire's note. Quick ask: can we firm up the downgrade credit mechanics and the seat-preservation language? Claire wants an explicit worked example that procurement can review. My suggested approach below; please comment or edit before I send back to Medistack.

Proposed mechanics (draft):
1) Pro-rata credit: calculate remaining committed dollar value (RemainingTermMonths / TotalCommittedMonths * CommittedARR) and apply as a credit against future invoices. Example: 12-month Core+ at $120k ARR. Downgrade at month 2 (10 months remaining) => credit = (10/12) * $120k = $100k, applied to subsequent invoices as a flat credit until exhausted.
2) Migration credit: one-time implementation credit to cover rollback friction. I was thinking 10% of committed ARR for the first year if downgrade occurs within the first 90 days.
3) Seat preservation: preserve user mappings for 180 days; after that, archived mappings can be restored with a re-onboarding fee.
4) Data retention: cached KV will be retained for 30 days post-downgrade; logs will be retained per our standard retention policy unless customer purchases extended retention.

Marissa — does Finance sign off on a 10% migration credit? If not, what level do you recommend? Also need confirmation that pro-rata credit treatment matches billing system constraints (we can't issue negative invoices; must show as credit balance).

Karthik — recommended negotiation play? Do we keep the 72-hour enact SLA?

Thanks —
Soojin

---
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>, karthik_iyer@redwood.com
Date: Fri, 07 Aug 2026 09:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Fwd: Plan simplification + rollback play for Medistack — need final guidance on credits/retention

Hi team — quick responses inline: 

- Migration credit: recommend 8% of committed ARR (not 10%). 8% is consistent with prior deals where we offered one-time operational credits.
- Pro-rata credit calc: we should avoid showing a huge one-time credit balance on the ledger. Instead, post the calculated credit to a credit balance account and automatically apply to invoices over the next 6 months (or until exhausted). That prevents negative invoice issues.
- Seat preservation: 180 days is fine. Add language that re-activation within 180 days incurs no additional provisioning fee; after 180 days a standard re-onboarding fee applies.
- Data retention: 30 days for KV caching is OK; however, for customers that need extended retention we should sell a 90-day add-on.

Also, recommend we tie the downgrade-trigger window: allowed within first 90 days for full migration credit; after 90 days, customers can still downgrade but forfeit the migration credit.

If Karthik agrees, I'll draft the final paragraph for the SOW and the credit language.

—Marissa
Director, Revenue Operations, Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com

Hi Claire — and hi Procurement team —

Thanks for the questions. We discussed internally and here is a concise worked example plus final proposed language to include in the SOW. If this looks good, we'll send the revised SOW and change order for signature.

Worked example (numbers):
- Committed plan: Core+ annual = $120,000 ARR (billed monthly = $10,000/mo).
- Downgrade occurs at day 45 (month 2) => 10 months remaining.
- Calculated pro-rata credit = (10/12) * $120,000 = $100,000 credit.
- How it's applied: Redwood posts the $100,000 to a credit balance on your account and automatically offsets monthly invoices up to 6 months (or until credit exhausted). This avoids negative invoice artifacts.
- Migration credit: Medistack is eligible for an 8% one-time migration credit on the committed ARR if the downgrade is requested within the first 90 days. For the example above: 8% * $120k = $9,600 credit, applied similarly to the credit balance.
- Seat preservation: Redwood will preserve user mappings and permissions for 180 days. Re-activation within 180 days: no provisioning fee. After 180 days: standard re-onboarding fee applies.
- Data retention: KV cache retained for 30 days by default; extended retention (90 days) available as a paid add-on. Audit logs retained per our standard retention and are available in Console.

Operational notes:
- Downgrade enactment SLA: Redwood will complete the downgrade within 72 hours of a signed change order, barring any customer-side provisioning dependencies.
- Billing cadence: you indicated a preference for monthly invoicing — we'll keep that by default.

Next steps:
1) If you accept the mechanics above, I will update the SOW and change order and circulate for signature.
2) Marissa will include the credit mechanics in payment terms.
3) We can schedule a 30-minute final review if procurement would like to walk through the numbers.

If you want the updated SOW attached directly in DocuSign, say the word and we’ll push that link.

Best,

— Soojin Lee
